title.en: Fraech's Fairy Raiment and the Host to Cruachan
title.zh: 弗蕾赫的仙衣與克魯阿坎之軍

region.zh: 愛爾蘭羅斯康芒郡克魯阿坎王陵

texts.period: Tain Bo Fraich (remscela to the Tain), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: To win Findabair, Fraech sends to his fairy kin, and from Boand his mother's sister at Mag Breg he receives the fairy splendour: black-blue mantles like a beetle's back, gold-looped tunics, fifty silver-rimmed shields, fifty grey mares with golden curbs and silver bells at every throat, seven chase-hounds linked in pairs by gold fetters holding bronze sheaths to their feet, and trumpeters with fairy-thread hair — so the host rides to Croghan, and the watchman swears no army so fair has come since Ailill first took the throne.
summary.zh: 為求娶芬娜芭爾，弗蕾赫遣使仙族求助；其姨母——女神博因——於瑪格·布雷格賜他仙家盛裝：甲蟲背般的黑藍斗篷、金環鑲邊的束衣、五十面銀緣盾、五十匹配金轡銀鈴的灰馬、以金鎖相連的七對獵犬與仙髮號手——大軍如此華美地馳向克羅漢堡，望樓哨兵斷言：自埃利爾登基以來，未見如此軍容。

sensitivity.note: The fairy-gift host is the classic entry set-piece of the Fraech tale (his Sid kindred on both sides — Bebind's sister is Boinn); cross-ref parallels: the marvellous a quoit-dropping of the Morrigan-Regamna woman and the Tuatha tribute-hosts. Pin is the real Rathcroghan royal site.

passages.text: Now the news of the love of that maid to Fraech, at his home where he dwelt, was brought, and they counselled him thus: "Let a message from thee be sent to thy fairy kin, to entreat their aid when we seek that maid; for the wondrous robes of the fairy land, and for gifts from the fairies plead." To Mag Breg, where his mother's sister dwelt, to Boand he away hath gone, and she gave to him mantles of dark black-blue, like a beetle's back they shone; four dark-grey rings in each cloak she gave were sewn, and a brooch shone bright with the good red gold in each mantle's fold; she gave tunics pale and white, and the tunics were bordered with golden loops, that forms as of beasts displayed; and a fifty she added of well-rimmed shields, that of silver white were made.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Fraich; not verbatim.

passages.text: By each of the fifty heroes' side was a sword with a hilt of gold, and a soft-grey mare was for each to ride, with a golden curb controlled; at each horse's throat was a silver plate, and a bell with a golden tongue swinging with a tinkling sound to the horse's tread. By their sides, seven chase-hounds were springing at leashes of silver they strained, and each couple a gold apple, swinging on the fetter that linked them, sustained; and their feet with bronze sheaths had been guarded. Seven trumpeters strode on the road before, and their hair, soft and yellow, like fairy threads, shone golden their shoulders round. All these were the gifts that the fairy gave, and gaily they made their start, and to Croghan's hold, in that guise so brave, away did the host depart. On the fort stands a watchman to view them, and thus news down to Croghan he calls: "Never army so fair nor so splendid yet hath come, nor its like shall be seen." And the youth before them, for his spear a full shot's length he flingeth, yet the spear never reacheth to ground, for his silver-chained hounds follow after, in their jaws is the spear ever found!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Fraich; not verbatim.

title.en: Eocho Bec and the Horses of the Sid
title.zh: 埃歐霍·貝克與仙族之馬

region.en: Sid Cuillne (fairy mound of Cuillne), Co. Limerick, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭利默里克郡庫爾涅仙丘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Dartada (remscela to the Tain), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: Eocho Bec son of Corpre, king of Cliu, keeper of forty fosterlings of Munster's kings, is visited in sleep by a woman of the mound of Cuillne: 'A stately troop shall be round thee, and goodly foreign horses under thee.' At dawn fifty black horses with gold and silver bridles stand tied to his gate, with fifty sets of Sid equipment, fifty white horses with red ears and purple manes, whips of white bronze with golden ends — the fairy debt owed him for defending their country and their soil.
summary.zh: 克利烏王科爾普雷之子埃歐霍·貝克，收養四十位芒斯特王子為養子；某夜庫爾涅仙丘的女子入夢相訪：「榮耀的隊伍將環繞你，異邦的駿馬將載你。」黎明時分，五十匹繫金銀轡的黑馬拴在他的堡門上，還有五十套仙家馬具、五十匹紅耳紫鬃的白馬、金端的白銅馬鞭——這是仙族對他守土之功的酬答。

sensitivity.note: The Sid-gift horses (white with red ears) are the fixed otherworld-horse motif of Irish legend, recurring from Land-under-Wave to the later fairy-steed tradition; the dream-counsel sets the remscela frame. Pin symbolic at the mound.

passages.text: EOCHO BEC, the son of Corpre, king of Cliu, dwelt in the Dun of Cuillne, and with him were forty fosterlings, all sons of the kings of Munster; he had also forty milch-cows for their sustenance. By Ailill and Medb messengers were sent, asking him to come to a conference. One night Eocho lay there in his sleep, when he saw something approach him; a woman, and a young man in her attendance. "Ye are welcome!" said Eocho. "It seems to me as if I had been near to you." "I think that we have been very near to one another, though we have not seen each other face to face!" "In what place do ye dwell?" "Yonder in Sid Cuillne, the fairy mound of Cuillne. In order to give thee counsel we are come: something that will bring thee honour and renown on thy journey at home and abroad. A stately troop shall be round thee, and goodly foreign horses shall be under thee."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Dartada; not verbatim.

passages.text: To-morrow in the morning fifty black horses, furnished with bridles of gold and silver, shall come to thee from me; and all of thy foster-children shall go with thee; well it becomes us to help thee, because thou art valiant in the defence of our country and our soil." Early in the morning they arise, there they see something: the fifty black horses, furnished with bridles of gold and silver tied fast to the gate of the castle, also fifty breeches of silver with embellishment of gold; and fifty youths' garments with their edges of spun gold, and fifty white horses with red ears and long tails, purple-red were all their tails and their manes, with foot-chains of brass upon each horse; there were also fifty whips of white bronze (findruine), with end pieces of gold.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Dartada; not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven Maine and the Cattle of Regamon

region.en: Burg of Regamon, Corcomroe, Co. Clare, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克萊爾郡科爾科姆羅伊雷加蒙堡

texts.period: Tain Bo Regamon (remscela to the Tain), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: Regamon of Connaught has seven fair daughters, and the seven Maine — sons of Ailill and Medb, named for their mixtures of their parents' natures — love them. Medb sends her sons for cattle, telling them to go for filial love; but at the water-springs Mani Mingar draws his sword on three of the maidens, and 'Give life for life!' wins three full words that cannot be cows — the pretence of courtship turned cattle-raid, and the tale that schools the Tain's logic of ransom and bride-price.
summary.zh: 康諾特的雷加蒙有七位美女兒；埃利爾與梅芙的七子——「七梅恩」，其名各自熔鑄父母之性——皆愛慕她們。梅芙遣子求牛，囑以「親愛之名」出行；然在水泉邊，明加爾竟向三位少女拔劍，「以命換命！」逼得三個誓言——卻偏偏不得是牛。求愛之名成為劫牛之實，此篇遂為《奪牛記》贖金與聘禮邏輯的序章。

sensitivity.note: The life-for-life exchange (a réir for a réir) is an Irish legal formula here dramatised as courtship; the seven sons' mixed-nature bynames (like his father, like his mother, mouth of honey) are genealogical byname practice. Pin at the traditional Corcomroe location.

passages.text: In the time of Ailill and Medb, a glorious warrior and holder of land dwelt in the land of Connaught, and his name was Regamon. He had many herds of cattle, all of them fair and well-shaped: he had also seven daughters with him. Now the seven sons of Ailill and Medb loved these daughters: namely the seven Maine — Maine Morgor (Maine with great filial love), Maine Mingar (Maine with less filial love), Maine Aithremail (Maine like his father), Maine Mathremail (Maine like his mother), Maine Milbel (Maine with the mouth of honey), Maine Moepert (Maine too great to be described), Maine Condageb-uile (Maine who combined all qualities): now this one had the form both of father and mother. The seven daughters of Regamon were the three Dunann, and the four Dunlaith; from the names of these is the estuary of Dunann in western Connaught.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamon; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now at a certain time, Ailill and Medb and Fergus held counsel together: "Some one from us should go to Regamon, that a present of cattle may be brought to us from him, to meet the need that there is on us for feeding the men of Ireland, when the kine are raided from Cualgne." "I know who would be good to go thither, if we ask it of them; even the Maine; on account of their love for the daughters." "Grateful is he, and a better journey does he go, who goes for the sake of his filial love." They set out, seven times twenty heroes was the number, till they were in the south of Connaught, near to the burg. Mani Mingar, with two others, went until he came upon three of the maidens at the water-springs, and at once he and his comrades drew their swords against them. "Give life for life!" said the maiden. "Grant to me then my three full words!" "Whatever thy tongue sets forth shall be done, only let it not be cows, for these have we no power to give thee." "For these indeed is all that now we do."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamon; not verbatim.

title.en: Flidais and Her Cow That Milked Three Hundred Men
title.zh: 弗蕾丹與供三百人飲奶的神牛

region.en: Dun of Ailill the Fair, Co. Mayo, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭梅奧郡「俊美埃利爾」之堡（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Flidais (remscela to the Tain; oldest recension LU), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: Flidais, wife of Ailill the Fair, loves Fergus mac Roich for the great deeds told of him, and keeps a marvellous cow that gives milk to more than three hundred men at one night's milking. Bricriu carries her message, and Fergus rides as ambassador — all the Ulster exiles with him — to carry off Flidais and her cow; the tale has two quite different endings in its manuscripts, and the Glenn Masain version makes Bricriu, the buffoon, a chief ollave whose satire on Fergus's broken promises is bitter and dignified.
summary.zh: 「俊美埃利爾」之妻弗蕾丹因聞芬恩·羅赫的英雄事跡而心生愛慕；她飼有一頭神牛，一夜之奶可供三百餘人。布里克留為信使傳話，芬恩以使者之名出行——阿爾斯特流亡者全數隨行——劫走弗蕾丹與神牛。此篇在手稿中有截然不同的兩種結局；而在格倫·馬辛本中，丑角布里克留化身首席詩人，諷刺芬恩背棄諾言之詩莊嚴而刻毒。

sensitivity.note: The wonder-cow (supplying a host) parallels Goibniu's ale and Manannan's self-renewing pigs — the otherworld-foodstuff family; the two-ending MS tradition is unique in Irish romance and is documented in the source's own introduction. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: The Tain bo Flidais, the Driving of the Cows of Flidais, occurs in both the two oldest collections of Old Irish romance, the Leabhar na h-Uidhri, and the Book of Leinster, besides the fifteenth century Egerton MS. After the dialogue with Fergus, Bricriu, with the poets that attend him, undertakes a journey to Ailill the Fair, to obtain from him the bounty that Fergus had promised but was unable to grant; he is received hospitably, and gets all he had asked for. He then asks about Ailill's wife Flidais, and is told about her marvellous cow, which was able to supply milk to more than three hundred men at one night's milking. Flidais returns from a journey, is welcomed by Bricriu, who produces a poem in honour of her and her cow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Flidais; not verbatim.

passages.text: A long conversation is then recorded between Flidais and Bricriu, in which Bricriu extols the great deeds of Fergus, supplying thereby a commentary on the short statement at the beginning of the older version, that Flidais' love to Fergus was on account of the great deeds which had been told her that he had done. Flidais declares to Bricriu her love for Fergus, and Bricriu consents to bring a message to Fergus that Flidais and her cow will come to him if he comes to her husband's castle to seek her. Bricriu induces him to go in the guise of an ambassador to Ailill the Fair, with the secret intention of carrying off Flidais; Fergus receives the sanction of Maev and her husband for his errand, and departs with all the Ulster exiles with him. And the Glenn Masain version makes Bricriu, who is a subordinate character in the older version, one of the principal actors: "Fergus, hear thy friend lamenting! Blunted is thy lofty mind; Thou, for hire, to Maev consenting, Hast thy valour's pride resigned."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Flidais; not verbatim.

title.en: The Red Woman of Regamna and the Cow of Cualnge
title.zh: 雷加姆納的紅衣女子與庫爾涅母牛

region.en: Ath da Ferta (Ford of the Two Marvels), Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡「雙異渡口」（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Regamna (also Tain bo Morrigna; LU-YBL recension), Heroic Romances of Ireland vol. II, trans. A. H. Leahy (1905)

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, vol. II (1905), eBook #5679

summary.en: A cry out of the north-west wakes Cuchulain at Dun Imrid, and he follows it to the Ford of the Double Wonder, where a chariot drawn by a one-legged chestnut horse with the pole driven through its body draws near: a red woman with crimson eyebrows, and a giant goading a cow before them. Their names are riddles of the Morrigan's satirical spells — she drives home as fee a marvellous poem — and when Cuchulain springs at her with spear and threats, the woman, the horse, the chariot, the cow and the man vanish, leaving the doom of the Brown Bull foretold.
summary.zh: 西北傳來的怪叫驚醒杜恩·伊姆里德的庫丘林；他循聲至「雙異渡口」，見一輛由三足獨腿栗色馬拖曳的戰車——車轅竟貫穿馬身——紅衣赤眉的女子與趕牛的巨人行於其前。二人名諱皆為摩里岡諷咒之謎——她以一首奇詩為酬，趕牛回家。庫丘林持矛躍起威嚇，女子、馬、車、牛與人霎時俱隱，庫爾涅褐牛的厄運已被預言。

sensitivity.note: Windisch conjectures the true title is Tain bo Morrigna, 'the driving of the Morrigan' — the red woman is the war-goddess herself in one of her forms; the one-legged horse and pole-through-body are the fixed marvel-chariot of her epiphanies, and the fee-for-a-poem is a reversal of the poet-fee custom. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: AT Dun Imrid lay Cuchulain, and slept, when a cry rang out; and in fear he heard from the north-land come ringing that terrible shout: He fell, as he woke from his slumber, with the thud of a weight, to the ground... Then he saw his harnessed chariot, and Laeg, his charioteer, from the north the car drew near: "And whence was the cry thou hast heard?" "From the north-west quarter it travelled, it crossed the great Cayll Cooen road!" "Follow on, on that track, till we know what that clamour may bode!"
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamna; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the ford of the Double Wonder, at Ath Fayrta, the car made stand, for a chariot rattled toward them from the clay-soiled Coolgarry land; and strange was the sight they saw: for a one-legged chestnut charger was harnessed the car to draw, and right through the horse's body the pole of the car had passed. A red woman sat in the chariot, bright red were her eyebrows twain, a crimson cloak was round her; and close by the side of that woman a mighty giant strode, on his back a staff of hazel, two-forked, and a cow he goaded, that shambled on before. "Ye who drive that cow do wrong, for against her will do ye drive her!" "Not to thee doth that cow belong. The kine of the land of Ulster are mine to guard!" "Dost thou sit on the seat of judgment? Too great is that task for thee!" "I of late made a marvellous poem; and as fee for the poem this cow do I drive to my home."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamna; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Cuchulain sprang at the chariot: "Would ye make me a fool with your jest?" He cried, as he leapt at the woman; his feet on her shoulders he pressed, and he set on her head his spear-point: "Now cease from thy sharp weapon-play!" "Then remove thyself from me! I am skilled in satirical spells." And the woman her song then sang, and the song was a song of insult. Again at the car he sprang, but nothing he found before him: as soon as the car he had neared, the woman, the horse, and the chariot, the cow, and the man disappeared.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905, vol. II, Tain bo Regamna; not verbatim.
